meta.description: Yes, it’s really Bulwer-Lytton — from his 1839 play Richelieu. But the popular one-liner trims a three-line verse: “…which Fate reserves / For a bright manhood…”

meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Bulwer-Lytton, from Richelieu (1839) — but the familiar line is a trimmed version of a longer verse spoken by the Cardinal.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1803–1873 · English novelist, playwright & politician (1st Baron Lytton)
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Bulwer-Lytton’s — but the familiar one-liner is a trimmed-down version of a three-line verse from his historical play Richelieu; or, The Conspiracy (1839). The full passage reads “In the lexicon of youth, which Fate reserves / For a bright manhood, there is no such word / As ‘fail.’”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Verse play in five acts, first performed 7 March 1839
Commonly cited as Act III, Scene I (some editions list Act II)

source.excerpt: In the lexicon of youth, which Fate reserves / For a bright manhood, there is no such word / As ‘fail.’
trail: The full passage — “which Fate reserves / For a bright manhood” and all — is preserved on Wikiquote, sourced to Richelieu (1839).
QuotePark attributes the same three-line wording to Richelieu, Act III, Scene I (1839).
The play is the same one that gave English “the pen is mightier than the sword” (Act II, Scene II) — both are genuine Bulwer-Lytton coinages from 1839.
source.excerptNote: The lines are spoken by the Cardinal Richelieu, urging on the young hero Adrien de Mauprat. The circulated quote drops the middle clause, turning a three-line blank-verse speech into a flat aphorism.
source.rightsNote: Richelieu; or, The Conspiracy was first published and performed in 1839, so both the play and this passage are in the public domain in the United States.

author.heading: About Edward Bulwer-Lytton
author.bio: Edward Bulwer-Lytton, 1st Baron Lytton, was one of the best-selling and most quotable authors of the Victorian era. His 1839 verse play Richelieu; or, The Conspiracy alone gave English several enduring phrases — “the pen is mightier than the sword” and this line about youth and failure among them. He also coined “It was a dark and stormy night,” which is why an annual bad-prose contest bears his name.

misattribution.heading: About the wording
misattribution.intro: The author is right — but the sentence you usually see has been quietly edited. The circulated one-liner drops a clause and flattens Bulwer-Lytton’s blank verse into prose.

items.who: “In the lexicon of youth there is no such word as fail”
items.why: This condensed version omits the middle of the original: “which Fate reserves / For a bright manhood.” The full three-line passage appears on Wikiquote, sourced to Richelieu (1839).
In the play the words are spoken by the Cardinal Richelieu to spur the young hero Adrien de Mauprat — a dramatic pep-talk, not a stand-alone maxim, as the sourced passage shows.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Bulwer-Lytton, genuinely from Richelieu (1839) — just remember the popular version is a trimmed quotation of a longer verse (Wikiquote).

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: Richelieu was a hit of the Victorian stage, and its most portable lines — this one and “the pen is mightier than the sword” — escaped the theatre to become common currency. Stripped of its verse and its speaker, the youth-and-failure line reads like a pure motivational slogan, which is exactly how it now circulates on posters and social feeds.
